question: What is the meaning of scenario modelling in relation to interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)?
data_group: interactive decision support tools (tools that support exploration and decision-making in ce object governance)
description: Scenario modelling in the context of passports and interactive decision support tools is a method that allows users to explore and reason about unknown future states of an object. This process supports the decision-making in circular economy (CE) object governance by enabling stakeholders to anticipate and plan for various potential outcomes and their implications. Scenario modelling helps in identifying a circular economy governance strategy by considering different future scenarios and their impact on the object and the overall system. This approach aids in making informed decisions that align with CE principles and objectives.

3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7). This view categorizes the management of a product 
life cycle from the environmental point of view into five phases: (1) raw 
material extraction, (2) manufacturing, (3) transportation, (4) utiliza­
tion (including maintenance), and (5) disposal or recycling. We have 
grouped identified roles based on similar function which resulted in 
twelve actor types that typically interact with a passport (see Fig. 6). 
These roles operate in four distinctive information chains grouped by 
information type: (1) the owners’ chain, (2) the governance chain, (3) 
the financial chain, and (4) the production chain. In the owners’ chain, 
we observe actors that are assigned with the majority of legal re­
sponsibilities for an object, i.e., either by owning it, leasing it or when 
assigned this responsibility from the owner (e.g., facility managers). The 
key objective for these actors is to have access to information that 
support the decision-making regarding the optimal acquiring and 
maintenance of an object according to the needs of the end-user. The 
governance chain is concerned with the task of securing the supply 
system in which the passport is used by verifying the quality, integrity, 
and validity of the information registered in or made accessible by 
passports. In this role of gatekeeper, we typically find the government, 
independent auditors, and passport software providers. The financial 
chain is concerned with financing and insuring an object. The key 
objective is to ensure a correct valuation of an object in order to identify 
the corresponding risk or to determine financing premiums. Finally, the 
production chain is mainly responsible for the physical life cycle oper­
ations performed on the object. This varies from material supply to 
design, production, assembly, distribution, maintenance and disman­
tling activities. The key objective of this group of actors is to document 
their activities in order that others later may benefit from this infor­
mation (including themselves, e.g., in maintenance activities). 
When considering the key opportunities and the key barriers (listed 
unweighted in Table A7, Appendix 5) we observe a misalignment be­
tween the stakes and challenges of different actors; some actors mainly 
benefit while others are charged with data registration and management 
costs. This observation is shared among other studies (e.g., Adisorn et al. 
(2021); Bouwend Nederland (2020); Debacker and Manshoven (2016); 
Greer et al. (2020); Munaro and Tavares (2021)). In some cases, there 
may even be adversarial thoughts against a passport as an information 
gain for one actor may lead to a deterioration of the negotiation position 
of another actor (e.g., recyclers). More generally, the majority of studies 
report that a passport facilitates environmental gains, and often also 
financial gains, hence, observe a societal-cost-benefit business case for 
implementing passports. 
3.8. Goals 
The ’identification of reuse value in the product’ is listed as the 
primary goal of a passport. A major part of this particular goal originates 
from papers related to the BAMB research project (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016), but it is used also extensively in direct phrasing or 
similar wording in other projects (Bertino et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019; 
Merrild et al., 2016; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).

cussions in the Information Systems field on design principles. Design 
principles are understood as prescriptive knowledge that specifies how 
to achieve goals in sociotechnical systems, highlighting the role of both 
human actors and technical mechanisms (Gregor et al., 2020). Recent 
work has also emphasized the need for systematic approaches to the 
development of design principles, ensuring they are both rigorous and 
applicable across diverse contexts (M¨oller et al., 2020). Positioning our 
design considerations within this line of thinking reinforces their role as 
actionable guidance, connecting systems engineering perspectives with 
established streams of design science research. By following these design 
considerations, companies can develop DPPs aligned with their CE 
strategies and capable of delivering the desired benefits in terms of 
transparency, efficiency, and sustainability. This approach ensures that 
DPPs are implemented effectively and contribute to the broader goals of 
the CE. These design considerations cover the second research question 
by focusing on how to design effective DPPs.
4.6. Practical implementation of DPP from a systems perspective
As highlighted by Thuesen et al. (2022) implementing DPPs effec­
tively requires a cohesive and adaptive strategy that considers the re­
lationships within the ecosystem. This begins with a thorough 
understanding and governance of the system, identifying the in­
terconnections, boundaries, and causal effects that define its operations. 
Mapping stakeholders, their roles, and the data flow they depend on 
establishes a foundation that fosters trust and accountability. Building 
on this foundation, it is critical to assess current system performance and 
circular operations and define complications or gaps. This includes 
evaluating technological possibilities and user needs to formulate soci­
etal and business cases for intervention, such as addressing interopera­
bility challenges or enhancing material recovery rates.
The process then progresses to identifying and developing viable 
solutions, where projects and experiments are organized to explore and 
refine potential outcomes. Pilot implementations play an important role, 
enabling controlled testing of functionalities and stakeholder collabo­
ration models while providing insights for scalability. To ensure long- 
term value delivery, the system must embed both standardization and 
flexibility, accommodating evolving needs without compromising on 
reliability or relevance. Stakeholder engagement is a vital element 
throughout the process, navigating complex dynamics and fostering 
dialogue to align expectations and maximize shared benefits (Thuesen 
et al., 2022). Complementary to our design considerations, recent 
research by Gieβ and M¨oller (2025) provides a value ecosystem 
perspective on DPPs. By applying e3-value modeling, they make explicit 
the transactional and informational relationships among actors across 
the product lifecycle. This abstraction is valuable for identifying 
ecosystem-level coordination requirements and reinforcing our findings 
related to strategic alignment and collaborative value creation. Reich 
et al. (2025) has similarly argued for moving beyond compliance by 
framing DPPs as value-creating, service-oriented, and integrated sys­
tems. Their emphasis on service orientation and integration comple­
ments our study, which advances five systems design considerations 
from a socio-technical and systems engineering perspective. While both 
approaches underline the need to broaden the role of DPPs, our 
contribution lies in articulating design considerations that specifically 
address alignment, data requirements, interoperability, tailoring to 
circular practices, and collaboration.
While some of the themes identified, such as the need for standards 
or the potential contribution of DPPs to CE outcomes, have been noted in 
prior studies, this study synthesizes these dispersed insights into five 
systems design considerations. By articulating these considerations, 
strategic alignment, data requirements, interoperability, tailoring to 
circular practices, and enabling collaboration, the study provides 
structured and prescriptive guidance for designing DPPs. This systems 
perspective extends existing research by moving beyond descriptive 
accounts and offering actionable insights that can inform both scholarly 
debates and practical implementation. By applying this integrated 
approach, DPP systems can transform from conceptual frameworks into 
operational tools that address immediate challenges while contributing 
to CE strategies.
